catalog_quote: Stress Alternation. Word-level stress in Bulgarian is not predictable – in some words it falls on the first syllable, in some on the final syllable, in others somewhere in between. It is thus phonemic, capable of distinguishing words from one another (e.g. кола 'car' – кола 'soda'; ударен 'stressed (masculine singular)' – ударен 'capable/efficient (masculine singular)'). It also is not uncommon for stress to shift within inflectional or derivational paradigms, resulting in variant forms of morphemes based on the presence or absence of stress. ... In nominal inflection it is quite common for a non-suffixed masculine noun root to be stressed in the singular, but not in the plural. ... Extensive lists of masculine and neuter nouns with their stress patterns can be found in Scatton 1984 (427-434). ... There is much less shifting of stress in feminine nouns. Most notable is the shift of stre…
sweep_summary: Bulgarian (bulg1262) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Leafgren 2011. The four title-keyword items split as follows. (1) Dimitrova et al. 2018 (Speech Prosody) fetched sources open from the ISCA archive and read in full: an age-variation study of intonation, phrasing and pauses; silent on word-stress placement, priority none. (2) Franks 2008 (JSL 16) is about clitic-cluster placement and its prosody, not lexical stress; Project MUSE paywall, no OA copy anywhere (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2/CORE/JSL OJS archive checked); low priority. (3) Bidwell 1968 (Studies in Linguistics 20:41-47) is a dedicated noun-stress study but print-only: archive.org's microfilm run lacks vol. 20 and HathiTrust was bot-blocked; medium priority as it would refine the lexical coding with noun pattern classes. (4) Grigorjan 1976 (Zeitschrift fur Slawistik 21:738-741, German) treats words with double/variable stress in the literary language - a refinement within a lexical system; De Gruyter paywalled, low priority. No sweep item contradicts the catalog. The best first-hand statement read is Patseva ROA-1612 p. 5 ('defined traditionally as free... cannot be inferred directly by the phonetic and morphological structure of the word'), confirming 'lexical'; it and Ternes & Vladimirova-Buhtz 1990 (minimal pair para 'steam' / para 'coin') were already on file from the 9/16 pass and do not supersede Leafgren.org, ISCA and search-engine HTML (mostly blocked or off-target).

new_statements.quote: Bulgarian accent has been defined traditionally as free. The place of the word stress has been considered a result of historical regularities, which have acted in the past and have been changed. Today, the lexical accent cannot be inferred directly by the phonetic and morphological structure of the word (Tilkov & Bojadžiev 2013: 156). According to the traditional Bulgarian linguistics the word stress can appear on almost any syllable of the word, as well as on various morphological units like prefixes, roots, suffixes and articles.
new_statements.citation: Patseva, Mirena. Bulgarian word stress analysis in the frame of prosody morphology interface. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-1612 (cited as 2017).
new_statements.locator: PDF p. 5, section 2.2 'Characteristics of Bulgarian lexical accent, accepted traditionally'
new_statements.reading: Free (unpredictable) lexical stress: it can fall on almost any syllable and is not derivable from phonological or morphological shape; consistent with the catalog's 'lexical' coding. Ternes & Vladimirova-Buhtz 1990 (JIPA 20(1):46, on file) independently gives the minimal pair ['pare] 'steam' / [pe'ra] 'coin' under 'Stress is distinctive'. None of the four sweep items yielded a readable stress-placement statement; this is the best first-hand statement read during the sweep, but it was fetched sources on 9/16 and should not be counted as a new find.

new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Locator correction only: the quoted heading 'Characteristics of Bulgarian lexical accent, accepted traditionally' is section 2 (parent); the passage sits under its subsection 2.2 'Positional characteristics', PDF/printed p. 5. The quote joins two paragraphs (break after '(Tilkov & Bojadžiev 2013: 156).'). Bearing unchanged: free, distinctive, unbounded lexical stress = catalog 'lexical'; corroborates, does not supersede, Leafgren 2011.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Leafgren 2011 text at the stated place (Ch. 2 'Stress Alternation', running pp. 19-21; txt lines 777ff). (2) Deciding source is a 2011 open-access concise grammar (82 pp.) — a sketch-level work, not the fullest description (Scatton 1984; Tilkov & Boyadzhiev; Academy Grammar 1982, none open), but the coded fact (free, phonemic, paradigmatically mobile stress = LEXICAL) is uncontroversial. (3) Two open sources fetched sources now to the JIPA Illustration (Ternes & Vladimirova-Buhtz 1990, p. 46 'Stress is distinctive', para 'steam' vs para 'coin') confirms; Patseva's ROA-1612 stress monograph-length paper (p. 5: 'defined traditionally as free... cannot be inferred directly by the phonetic and morphological structure of the word'; system 'unbounded', penultimate as statistical default

sources.citation: Dimitrova, Snezhina; Andreeva, Bistra; Gabriel, Christoph; Grünke, Jonas. 2018. Speaker age effects on prosodic patterns in Bulgarian. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2018 (Poznań), 709-713.
sources.quote: Both groups used the same inventory of pitch accents and boundary tones, but there were significant differences in the frequency counts of some of the tones: young speakers used pre-nuclear rises with a post-tonic high target, while older speakers preferred rises with a high target within the stressed syllable; the nuclear pitch accent used most frequently by the young speakers was L*, whereas the one preferred by the elderly speakers was L+H*
sources.note: Read in full. Compares two groups of six female Standard Bulgarian speakers (19-23 vs 79-88) reading The North Wind and the Sun: pitch span, F0 minimum, syllable/IP/pause duration, ToBI pitch-accent and boundary-tone inventories. 'Stressed syllable' appears only as the anchor of pitch accents (e.g. 'older speakers preferred rises with a high target within the stressed syllable'). No statement about where word stress falls or whether it is fixed or lexical.
